analysis.one_liner: Makes it a federal crime for a sitting President or Vice President to interfere in an election.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee for 16 months and died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended existing federal law that bars federal employees from interfering in elections, adding the President and Vice President by name. It would have banned them from using their authority to interfere with or affect an election, barred them from coercing political activity, and raised the maximum prison sentence for the offense from one year to three years. The bill was introduced in August 2021, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, later sent to a crime subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters would benefit from a clear federal criminal prohibition on the two most powerful officials in the executive branch using their office to affect an election outcome, backed by a three-year maximum prison term. It also protects candidates and campaigns from coercion of political activity by the President or Vice President.

how_it_helps.text: It closes a gap in the criminal code: the existing law against election interference by federal officials did not name the President or Vice President, and this bill adds them explicitly.
It raises the maximum prison term for the offense from one year to three years, giving the prohibition real teeth.
It also bars a President or Vice President from coercing political activity, extending protections already applied to other federal employees.

analysis.who_pays: Incumbent presidents and vice presidents would bear the new legal exposure: conduct that was not clearly criminal for them before would carry up to three years in prison.

drawbacks.text: Tripling the maximum prison term from one to three years is a significant criminal penalty increase, and opponents of expanding criminal statutes generally argue such escalation should be reserved for clearly warranted cases.
The bill reaches not only the President and Vice President but also a broad class of executive branch officials and government employees, so its scope is wider than its title suggests.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: existing law barred federal employees from interfering in elections but said nothing about the President or Vice President themselves, and the cost of closing it was minimal. The main objection is practical — a criminal statute aimed at the President raises constitutional enforcement questions and covers conduct some would argue is already addressed through impeachment — but the cost of adding it to the criminal code is small, so the loss of a cheap, narrow safeguard falls on the public.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee referred the bill to a crime subcommittee, which never acted, so it died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 23, 2021 and referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day.

More than a year later, on November 1, 2022, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — with only months left in the Congress and no evidence of a markup or hearing in the record.
No further action was taken, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent presidents and vice presidents remain free from criminal liability for election interference under the general federal interference statute, and the sitting executive branch avoided any new constraint on its actions.

for.name: Rep. Hank Johnson of Georgia, Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee, Rep. Eric Swalwell, Rep. Mondaire Jones, Rep. Pramila Jayapal, and Rep. Eleanor Holmes Norton

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out; it sat referred for 16 months until the Congress ended.

against.name: House Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on November 1, 2022 and held no recorded action on it before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 6 cosponsors were House Democrats, and the bill died in a House committee without ever reaching the floor, so support was one-sided from the start.

industries.industry: Incumbent presidents and vice presidents (and future officeholders)
industries.note: The bill would make the nation's top executives criminally liable — with up to three years in prison — for using their authority to affect an election, closing the personal gap in existing law.
